questions.stem: Entrepreneurship is best described as:
options: owning a business that has been handed down through several generations of a family
identifying an opportunity and taking on the risk of turning it into a new venture
managing the day-to-day operations of a long-established business efficiently
investing personal savings in the shares of companies listed on the stock exchange
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurship is the process of spotting an opportunity and accepting the risk of creating a new venture to pursue it. Running the daily operations of an existing business is the role of a manager, which is related but does not involve creating something new.

questions.stem: Priya, a nurse, notices that shift workers in Geelong cannot buy healthy meals at 3 am. She leaves her job and uses her savings to start a late-night healthy meal delivery service. Which feature of entrepreneurship does this most clearly show?
options: applying established procedures to coordinate an existing team
choosing a market in which there is no uncertainty about demand
securing a guaranteed income from a salaried position
accepting personal financial risk to act on an unmet need
questions.explanation: Priya gives up a secure income and commits her own savings to meet a need she has identified, which is the risk-taking at the heart of entrepreneurship. Coordinating an existing team using set procedures describes management of an established business, not the creation of a new one.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a business entrepreneur from a business manager?
options: An entrepreneur is motivated only by profit; a manager is motivated only by meeting the needs and wishes of staff.
An entrepreneur creates and takes the risk of a new venture; a manager coordinates resources to achieve an existing business's objectives.
An entrepreneur focuses on day-to-day operations and routines; a manager focuses on creating new ventures, taking risks and generating new ideas.
An entrepreneur must hold a formal business qualification; a manager learns the role only through experience on the job.
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurs bring new ventures into being and carry the risk of doing so, while managers coordinate people and resources to achieve the objectives of a business that already exists. The reversed version swaps the two roles, and neither role requires a particular qualification.

questions.stem: Tom has worked for an engineering firm for 15 years. He starts his own consultancy mainly so that he can choose his own projects and working hours. His main motivation is:
options: fulfilling a market need
making a profit for shareholders
personal independence
fulfilling a social need
questions.explanation: Wanting to choose his own projects and hours rather than follow an employer's directions is the desire for personal independence. Nothing in the scenario suggests he is responding to an unmet market or social need, and a consultancy he owns has no outside shareholders.

questions.stem: Lena starts a café in Footscray that employs and trains young refugees, reinvesting its surplus in the training program. Her main motivation is to:
options: achieve personal independence from an employer
maximise the profit returned to her as the owner
fulfil a social need
gain financial independence through a high personal income
questions.explanation: Lena reinvests the surplus in training young refugees, so her primary purpose is meeting a social need. A business that channels its surplus back into its program rather than to its owner is not driven mainly by personal income or profit.

questions.stem: Starting a business to fulfil a market need means setting it up to:
options: work flexible hours chosen by the owner rather than by an employer
earn a return on the owner's savings higher than a bank account pays
supply a good or service that customers want but cannot readily obtain
provide a service to a disadvantaged group without expecting any revenue
questions.explanation: A market need is a demand from customers that is not currently being met, and a business can be started to fill it. Providing a service to a disadvantaged group is a social need, and choosing one's own hours is personal independence.

questions.stem: Making a profit as a motivation for starting a business means the owner aims to:
options: pay its staff higher wages than any competitor operating in the same industry
set prices below costs so the business can win market share
reinvest every dollar of revenue into a chosen social cause
earn revenue that is greater than the costs of running the business
questions.explanation: Profit is the amount by which revenue exceeds expenses, so a profit motive means aiming for revenue above costs. Pricing below costs produces a loss, and reinvesting all revenue in a cause describes a social motive rather than a profit motive.

questions.stem: Which characteristic is most typical of a successful business entrepreneur?
options: a reluctance to change a proven approach
a strong dislike of uncertainty and ambiguity
a willingness to take calculated risks
a preference for stable, predictable routines
questions.explanation: Successful entrepreneurs are prepared to take risks that they have assessed and judged worth taking. A preference for routine and a dislike of uncertainty would make it hard to start a venture whose success is never guaranteed.

questions.stem: Marcus's bakery has twice failed to win a supermarket supply contract. He asks for feedback, changes his recipe and packaging, and applies again. Which characteristic is he showing most clearly?
options: resilience
delegation
risk aversion
conformity
questions.explanation: Resilience is the ability to recover from setbacks and keep working towards a goal, which Marcus shows by learning from rejection and trying again. Delegation means assigning tasks to others, which the scenario does not describe.

questions.stem: The manager of a Bendigo hardware store explains a new rostering system to staff, listens to their concerns and adjusts the roster. How does this characteristic most directly contribute to business success?
options: Communicating clearly removes any need for the manager to make further decisions about rosters in future.
Listening to staff means wage costs will fall, because staff will accept lower rates of pay in return.
Adjusting the roster shows creativity, which guarantees that the store will attract many new customers.
Two-way communication builds staff understanding and support, so the change is carried out more smoothly.
questions.explanation: Good communication means staff understand the reason for a change and feel heard, which makes them more likely to support it and less likely to resist. Communication does not end the need for future decisions, and it has no direct link to lower pay rates.

questions.stem: An entrepreneur who is highly creative but poor at planning launches a product that sells out within a week, then cannot meet demand for two months. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The business struggled because creativity is not a characteristic that contributes to the success of a business.
The shortage shows that market research was unnecessary, since demand turned out to be so strong.
Planning would have reduced demand, so the shortage was the best possible result for the business.
Creativity identified the opportunity, but weak planning limited how much the business could gain from it.
questions.explanation: The product's rapid sales show that the creative idea met a real demand, but without planning for supply the business lost two months of sales and possibly customers. Success usually needs a combination of characteristics, so creativity is valuable but not sufficient on its own.

questions.stem: An entrepreneur can describe clearly what her business will look like in five years and inspires her first employees to work towards it. Which characteristic is she showing?
options: risk aversion
technical expertise
attention to routine
vision
questions.explanation: Vision is the ability to picture a future for the business and communicate it in a way that motivates others. Technical expertise is skill in performing particular tasks, which the scenario does not mention.

questions.stem: Research and development (R&D) as a source of business opportunity involves:
options: surveying existing customers about how satisfied they are with the service provided
expanding sales of an unchanged product into overseas markets
systematic investigation to create new products, processes or knowledge
copying a competitor's product and selling it at a lower price
questions.explanation: R&D is planned, systematic work to discover new knowledge or develop new products and processes, which can open up opportunities for a business. Selling an unchanged product overseas is taking advantage of global markets, not R&D.

questions.stem: As more young Australians live in small inner-city apartments, a Ballarat furniture maker begins designing compact desks and fold-away tables. This opportunity has come mainly from:
options: technological development
changing customer needs
global markets
government grants
questions.explanation: The change in how people live has created a need for smaller furniture, so the opportunity comes from changing customer needs. The scenario involves no new technology and no overseas market, only a shift in what local customers require.

questions.stem: A Tasmanian honey producer learns that demand for Australian leatherwood honey is growing in Singapore, and begins exporting there. The source of business opportunity is:
options: technological development
changing customer needs in Tasmania
global markets
research and development
questions.explanation: Selling to customers in another country is taking advantage of global markets. The producer has not developed a new product or technology, and the change in demand is in Singapore rather than in Tasmania.

questions.stem: Which example best shows innovation as a source of business opportunity?
options: A Perth start-up develops an app that lets tradespeople quote for jobs from a photo.
A newsagent extends its opening hours so that they match the hours of a nearby competitor.
A clothing store holds its usual end-of-season clearance sale for winter stock.
A café owner renews the lease on the same premises for a further five years.
questions.explanation: Innovation is the creation of something new or the significant improvement of an existing product or process, such as a new way of quoting for jobs. Matching a competitor's hours or running a routine sale changes nothing new about what the business offers.

questions.stem: Low-cost drones become widely available. A Wagga Wagga pharmacy, which does no research of its own, buys several to deliver medicines to farms. The source of opportunity is best described as:
options: innovation by the pharmacy's own engineers, who designed the drones
technological development, because it applies technology developed by others
research and development, because the pharmacy has found a new use for a recent technology
global markets, because many of the drones are manufactured overseas
questions.explanation: The pharmacy is taking advantage of a technological development that has made drones cheap, without doing any research itself. R&D requires the business to carry out the systematic investigation, and the drones were not designed by the pharmacy.

questions.stem: Two Brisbane businesses both stop offering home delivery to the outer suburbs. A third business begins delivering to the suburbs they used to serve. This is best described as:
options: an opportunity created by the business's own research and development
an opportunity arising mainly from overseas markets and exporting
a change in customer needs caused by a new technological development
recognising and taking advantage of a market opportunity
questions.explanation: Customers' needs have not changed; what has changed is that competitors have left a gap, which the third business recognises and fills. No research, technology or overseas market is involved.

questions.stem: A SMART business goal is one that is:
options: simple, monitored, ambitious, realistic and targeted
significant, manageable, approved, resourced and trackable
specific, motivating, affordable, reviewed and timely
specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound
questions.explanation: SMART goals are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, which makes it clear what must be done and by when. A goal that is not measurable or has no deadline cannot be used to judge whether the business has succeeded.

questions.stem: Which goal is best written for a new surf school at Torquay?
options: Increase the number of students as much as is possible.
Enrol 300 students in lessons by the end of its first summer.
Become the most popular surf school anywhere on the coast.
Grow quickly over the next few years and keep customers happy.
questions.explanation: The best goal states a measurable target and a deadline, so the owner can tell whether it has been met. The other goals are vague, with no number or no time frame to measure performance against.

questions.stem: Why is goal setting important for a business in the planning stage?
options: It replaces decision-making, because staff only need to follow the set goals.
It gives direction and sets a standard against which performance can be measured.
It removes the need for market research, because targets have already been set.
It guarantees the business will make a profit in its very first year of operation.
questions.explanation: Goals tell owners and staff what the business is trying to achieve and allow results to be compared with targets. Setting a goal does not make it happen, and decisions are still needed about how to achieve it.

questions.stem: The owner of a new florist must choose between two possible shop locations. Which sequence best reflects a logical decision-making process?
options: identify the problem, gather information, consider alternatives, choose and implement, evaluate
choose and implement, gather information, identify the problem, evaluate, consider alternatives
consider alternatives, choose and implement, identify the problem, gather information, evaluate
gather information, evaluate, identify the problem, choose and implement, consider alternatives
questions.explanation: A logical decision starts by defining the problem and gathering information, then weighs the alternatives before choosing one, and finally evaluates the result. Choosing before gathering information or considering alternatives risks a poor decision that cannot be justified.

questions.stem: A new business sets the goal 'achieve a 10% profit margin in the first year'. After six months the margin is 3%. The owner's most appropriate next step is to:
options: abandon goal setting altogether, since this goal has proved to be unrealistic
keep operating unchanged, because goals can only be checked at the end of the year
cut prices straight away, because more sales will always raise the profit margin
evaluate why the result differs from the goal and consider alternative actions
questions.explanation: Comparing results with the goal part-way through allows the owner to find the cause of the gap and act on it while there is still time. Cutting prices may raise sales but lowers the margin on each sale, so it does not necessarily improve the profit margin.

questions.stem: Business concept development is the process of:
options: selling a business idea to an investor in exchange for shares in a newly formed company
measuring whether a business has met its objectives after its first year of trading
refining a business idea into a clear statement of what will be offered, to whom and how
registering a business name and obtaining an Australian Business Number for the business
questions.explanation: Concept development takes a raw idea and shapes it into a defined offering, a target market and a way of delivering it. Registering a name is a legal requirement that comes later, once the concept is settled.

questions.stem: Why is business concept development important before a business is established?
options: It sets the wages that staff will be paid under the relevant modern award.
It shapes the idea into an offering that customers will value and pay for.
It legally protects the idea so that competitors are unable to copy it.
It ensures the owner will not need any external finance to start trading.
questions.explanation: A raw idea needs to be developed into something customers want at a price they will pay, and doing this early reduces the risk of failure. Concept development gives no legal protection; that comes from intellectual property rights such as patents and trade marks.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between business opportunities and business concept development?
options: Once an opportunity is found, concept development is unnecessary because demand is already proven.
They are unrelated, because opportunities concern the market and concepts concern only finance.
Concept development is needed only when the opportunity comes from overseas markets.
An opportunity is the starting point, and concept development turns it into a workable offering.
questions.explanation: Concept development begins with an identified opportunity and works out how a business could take advantage of it. Spotting an opportunity does not show that a particular product, price or delivery method will succeed, so development is still needed.

questions.stem: Jade sees that many Darwin households want help cleaning their solar panels. She defines the service, sets prices for small and large roofs and decides to target homeowners in newer suburbs. Jade is now:
options: identifying a source of opportunity through research and development
evaluating the performance of the business against its SMART goals
developing a business concept from an identified opportunity
conducting a feasibility study of a completed business plan
questions.explanation: Jade has already found the opportunity and is now deciding what the service is, what it will cost and who it is for, which is concept development. A feasibility study would test whether this concept is viable, which she has not yet done.

questions.stem: Primary market research involves:
options: collecting new data first-hand, such as through surveys or focus groups
using data already published by others, such as census statistics
reading industry reports bought from a market research company
reviewing statistics published by a government agency
questions.explanation: Primary research gathers new information directly for the business's own purpose. Census statistics, purchased industry reports and other published data were collected by someone else, so they are secondary research.

questions.stem: The owner of a planned dog-grooming van in Launceston uses Australian Bureau of Statistics census data to estimate the number of households in the area. This is an example of:
options: qualitative research
observational research
secondary research
primary research
questions.explanation: Census data has already been collected and published by another organisation, so using it is secondary research. It is also quantitative, being counts of households, rather than qualitative data about opinions and reasons.

questions.stem: A focus group of eight parents discussing why they choose particular childcare centres would mainly produce:
options: qualitative data about attitudes and reasons
quantitative data suitable for estimating market share
secondary data collected by another organisation
financial data showing the centres' running costs
questions.explanation: Focus groups produce rich, descriptive information about why people think and act as they do, which is qualitative data. A group of eight is far too small and unstructured to produce reliable figures for market share.

questions.stem: An initial feasibility study assesses:
options: which staff should be promoted once the business has grown in size
the amount of tax a business owes at the end of a financial year
whether a business idea is likely to be viable before major resources are committed
how well an established business has met its objectives over the past year
questions.explanation: A feasibility study investigates whether an idea can work, covering the market, operations and finances, before the owner invests heavily. It looks forward at a proposed business, not backwards at the performance of one already operating.

questions.stem: Which question would most likely be answered by the financial part of an initial feasibility study?
options: Which advertising slogan will customers find easiest to remember?
Which modern award will cover the business's employees?
Will expected revenue cover start-up and running costs within a reasonable time?
Is there a large enough group of customers who would want to buy the product?
questions.explanation: The financial part of a feasibility study estimates costs and revenue to judge whether the business can become profitable and survive. Whether enough customers exist is a question for the market part of the study, not the financial part.

questions.stem: A survey of 200 Year 12 students finds that 70% would 'probably' buy a study-snack subscription at $15 a month. Before relying on this result, the entrepreneur should most consider that:
options: a result of 70% is high enough to guarantee the business will be profitable
stated intentions often overstate actual purchases, so further testing is needed
a sample of 200 is always too small to give any useful information at all
primary data is less reliable than secondary data in every situation
questions.explanation: People often say they would buy a product but do not do so when asked to pay, so a trial or pre-sale gives better evidence of real demand. A sample of 200 can be useful, and primary data is often more relevant than secondary data because it is collected for the business's own question.

questions.stem: Which is an economic contribution that businesses make to a nation?
options: creating employment and paying taxes that help fund public services
setting the interest rates that banks charge on business loans
passing the laws that protect consumers from unsafe goods
deciding the rate of unemployment benefits paid to job seekers
questions.explanation: Businesses employ people, produce goods and services and pay taxes, all of which add to a nation's economic wellbeing. Setting the cash rate is the role of the Reserve Bank, and laws and welfare payments are decided by parliaments and governments.

questions.stem: A Shepparton food manufacturer sponsors local junior sport and donates surplus stock to a food bank. These actions contribute mainly to:
options: the nation's balance of trade
the business's legal compliance
government tax revenue
social wellbeing in the community
questions.explanation: Supporting local sport and donating food improves quality of life in the community, which is social wellbeing. Neither action is required by law, and neither involves exporting or importing, so it does not affect the balance of trade.

questions.stem: How does a new business that introduces an innovative product contribute to economic wellbeing?
options: It lowers national living standards, because consumers spend a larger share of their income.
It adds to economic wellbeing only if it is a public listed company with shareholders.
It can increase competition, consumer choice and productivity, adding to economic growth.
It always reduces the total number of jobs, because innovation replaces workers with machines.
questions.explanation: New products give consumers more choice and push competitors to improve, which raises productivity and growth. Innovation can change the kinds of jobs available, but it does not always reduce total employment, and businesses of every structure contribute to the economy.

questions.stem: Which example shows a business contributing mainly to social wellbeing rather than to economic wellbeing?
options: A gym runs free classes for older residents to reduce their isolation.
A factory expands its output and pays more company tax as a result.
A mining company exports more iron ore, earning more foreign income.
A retailer increases its sales revenue by 15% compared with last year.
questions.explanation: Free classes that reduce isolation improve people's health and connection with their community, which is social wellbeing. Higher output, exports, tax and sales are measures of economic activity and contribute mainly to economic wellbeing.

questions.stem: Which is a method by which a culture of business innovation and entrepreneurship may be fostered in a nation?
options: school-based educational programs in entrepreneurship
a higher company tax rate for newly formed businesses
limits on the number of business names that can be registered
grants that are available only to long-established firms
questions.explanation: Teaching entrepreneurship in schools builds the knowledge, skills and confidence that young people need to start businesses. Higher taxes on new businesses or grants reserved for established firms would discourage rather than foster new ventures.

questions.stem: A regional council turns an empty building into a start-up hub with low-cost desks, fast internet and mentoring. The main way this fosters entrepreneurship is by:
options: protecting the hub's businesses from competitors outside the region
lowering start-up costs and connecting founders with support and with each other
guaranteeing that every business located in the hub will make a profit
removing the need for the hub's businesses to register or pay tax
questions.explanation: Start-up hubs reduce the cost and risk of starting out and give founders access to mentors, networks and shared facilities. They cannot guarantee success, and businesses in a hub must still meet every legal and tax requirement.

questions.stem: How does government investment in research and development help to foster business innovation?
options: It allows the government to take ownership of and run each new business that emerges from it.
It reduces business costs by setting a lower minimum wage for research staff.
It prevents overseas firms from selling competing products in Australia.
It creates new knowledge and technology that businesses can turn into new products.
questions.explanation: Publicly funded research, for example in universities and the CSIRO, produces knowledge and technology that businesses can commercialise. The government does not take ownership of the businesses that use this research.

questions.stem: A council offers $5,000 grants to people starting new businesses. Which evaluation of this policy is most valid?
options: It is ineffective, because only the federal government can foster entrepreneurship.
It eases start-up finance, but its effect depends on whether the funded ideas are viable.
It will certainly raise innovation, because any extra money given to founders always produces new ideas.
It cannot help, because a grant is a form of debt that must be repaid with interest.
questions.explanation: A grant reduces the amount a founder must borrow or save, but a grant alone cannot make a poorly conceived idea succeed. Grants do not have to be repaid, which is what makes them attractive, and councils are one of several levels that can foster entrepreneurship.
